title: US Green Card Approvals Drop 35% as Indian Applicants Bear the Brunt
excerpt: EB-1A approval rates for Indians fell sharply in FY26, with immigration attorneys warning of an 'unreasonably high bar' despite no change in law.
body:
• EB-1A green card approval rates for Indians dropped from 49.1% in FY25 to 35% in the first two quarters of FY26, according to USCIS data analyzed by Boundless Immigration.
  • Indian applicants filed 7,316 petitions in the first half of FY26, with only 2,571 approved and 1,131 denied — a sharp reversal from prior trends.
  • Immigration attorneys say adjudicators are demanding an "unreasonably high bar" despite no change in the underlying law.
  • With EB-2 and EB-3 backlogs stretching up to 15 years, Indian nationals are increasingly turning to EB-5 investment visas and talent visa programs in Canada and the UK.

Steep Decline in EB-1A Approvals

US green card approvals through the EB-1A extraordinary ability category have dropped 35% overall, with Indian applicants absorbing the heaviest losses, according to USCIS data analyzed by Boundless Immigration.

The approval rate for Indian EB-1A petitions fell from 49.1% in FY25 to just 35% in the first two quarters of FY26. During FY25, Indians filed 14,250 petitions and secured 6,993 approvals against 1,474 denials. In the first half of FY26 alone, 7,316 petitions yielded only 2,571 approvals, with 1,131 denied.

Immigration experts say the decline is most pronounced among Indian technology workers, followed by Chinese applicants, who file the largest EB-1A volumes globally.

A Higher Bar With No Legal Change

The drop comes amid tighter immigration adjudication under the Trump administration, though no statutory changes have been enacted for the EB-1A category.

"The spike in denials is not due to a drop in the calibre of applicants."

— Joel Yanovich, Senior Attorney, Ganey Law Group

Yanovich told the Economic Times that USCIS adjudicators are now demanding an "unreasonably high bar" from applicants. Boundless Immigration CEO Xiao Wang added that simply meeting three of the ten USCIS criteria — the statutory threshold — is no longer sufficient. Strong evidence in categories such as leading roles in distinguished organizations and commanding high salaries is now treated as baseline, with at least one additional high-quality criterion expected.

Immigration attorney Rajiv Khanna described the current adjudication environment as "extremely difficult," noting that courts have begun questioning the methodology USCIS officers use to evaluate EB-1A petitions.

Indian Applicants Explore Alternatives

The EB-1A squeeze adds pressure to an already difficult landscape for Indian nationals seeking permanent residence in the United States. Employment-based green card backlogs in the EB-2 and EB-3 categories stretch up to 15 years for Indian-born applicants — the longest wait times of any nationality.

Faced with these compounding obstacles, Indian professionals are exploring several alternative pathways:

  • EB-1C: Working abroad for a year in a managerial or executive capacity at a qualifying multinational company to establish eligibility.
  • EB-5: The investment-based immigration route, which has seen a notable surge in Indian applicants willing to commit the required capital.
  • Relocation: Moving to Canada or the United Kingdom, where talent visas such as Canada's Global Talent Stream and the UK's High Potential Individual visa offer more predictable timelines.

What It Means for the Diaspora

The decline hits at a particularly vulnerable moment for Indian tech workers in the US. Many entered the country on H-1B visas and have waited years — in some cases over a decade — for green card processing. A tightening EB-1A pathway removes what had been a faster alternative to the backlogged EB-2 and EB-3 queues.

For those already in the pipeline, the immediate impact is uncertainty. Pending petitions face the same higher scrutiny, and attorneys advise applicants to bolster their evidence packages significantly before filing.

Looking Ahead

Unless the policy environment shifts, experts warn that extraordinary-skilled workers — especially Indians — will continue to face mounting barriers to securing permanent residence in the United States. Several federal court challenges to USCIS adjudication practices are working through the system, and their outcomes could reset expectations for how the agency evaluates EB-1A petitions.

For now, the numbers paint a stark picture: the door to America's most prestigious employment-based green card is narrowing fastest for the country's largest applicant pool.
